title: Grounds of Judicial Review — Illegality, Irrationality (Wednesbury Unreasonableness), Procedural Impropriety

content.overview: Judicial review is the supervisory jurisdiction by which courts test the legality of administrative action. The classic grounds are illegality, irrationality (including Wednesbury unreasonableness), and procedural impropriety. Review examines the decision-making process and legal limits of power; it is not an appeal on the merits unless the statute so provides.
content.glance: Identify the power and decision; test jurisdiction and purpose (illegality); test rationality (irrationality / Wednesbury); test fairness of procedure (procedural impropriety); then formulate the precise remedy without substituting the court's preferred outcome.
content.study:
Core idea: judicial review polices the legal boundaries of public power. Courts ask whether the authority acted within jurisdiction, for a proper purpose, on relevant considerations, fairly, and rationally. They do not ordinarily redecide the administrative merits.

Illegality: The authority must correctly understand and apply the law that regulates its power. Acting outside jurisdiction, for an improper purpose, or on irrelevant considerations is illegal. Misconstruction of the enabling statute is a classic form of illegality.

Irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness): A decision is irrational if it is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. The threshold is high. Structured proportionality may apply with greater intensity where fundamental rights or severe burdens are engaged, but reasonableness and proportionality should not be collapsed into a single slogan.

Procedural impropriety: Fair procedure includes the rules of natural justice (audi alteram partem, nemo judex) and compliance with mandatory statutory procedure. Failure of notice, hearing, or bias rules can vitiate the decision even if the outcome might otherwise have been open.

Limits of review: Review is supervisory. The court quashes or remits where a legal defect is shown; it does not substitute its own policy preference. Alternative remedies, standing, and delay may affect maintainability.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in Articles 226 and 32/136 of the Constitution and in the specific statute creating the administrative power. Do not treat the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 as the source of judicial-review doctrine; evidence provisions apply only when proof issues arise.

sections.heading: Meaning and Purpose of Judicial Review
sections.body: Judicial review is the court's power to examine the legality of administrative action. Its purpose is to keep public authorities within the law, not to replace them as primary decision-makers on policy or merits.

sections.heading: Illegality
sections.body: Illegality covers excess of jurisdiction, misconstruction of the enabling law, improper purpose, and relevant/irrelevant considerations. The authority must correctly understand the legal limits of its power and apply them to the facts.

sections.heading: Irrationality and Wednesbury Unreasonableness
sections.body: A decision is irrational if it is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. The threshold is deliberately high. Where rights or severe interests are engaged, courts may apply a more structured proportionality analysis, but the intensity of review depends on context.

sections.heading: Procedural Impropriety
sections.body: Procedural impropriety includes breach of natural justice and failure to follow mandatory statutory procedure. Notice, hearing, and unbiased decision-making are central. A procedural defect can vitiate the decision independently of the merits outcome.

sections.heading: Remedies and Limits
sections.body: Typical relief is quashing and remittal for a lawful decision. Declaratory and mandatory relief may also be available. Courts respect alternative remedies, standing rules, and the distinction between legality review and merits appeal.

examples.title: Wrong purpose under the statute
examples.body: A licensing statute authorises refusal only on fitness grounds. The authority refuses a licence to pressure the applicant in an unrelated commercial dispute. The issue is illegality through improper purpose.

examples.title: Wednesbury challenge
examples.body: An authority cancels a benefit on grounds that no reasonable decision-maker, looking at the same material, could accept. The analysis must apply the high irrationality threshold and avoid pure merits disagreement.

examples.title: Hearing denied
examples.body: A statute requires notice and hearing before cancellation of a registration. The authority cancels without notice. Procedural impropriety is made out independently of whether cancellation might have been open on the merits.

hypotheticals.question: The court prefers a different policy outcome. Is that a ground of review?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Judicial review is not an appeal on merits. Identify a legal defect under illegality, irrationality or procedural impropriety. Disagreement with the policy choice is not enough.

hypotheticals.question: Are Wednesbury unreasonableness and proportionality the same?
hypotheticals.analysis: Not identical. Wednesbury asks whether the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. Proportionality is a structured means-ends inquiry. Indian courts use both approaches depending on context and the rights engaged.

distinctions.title: Judicial review vs appeal on merits
distinctions.left: Review tests legality of the decision-making process and power.
distinctions.right: An appeal redecides the merits where the statute confers appellate power.

rows.left: Supervisory: jurisdiction, purpose, considerations, fairness, rationality.
rows.right: Appellate: substitute the correct decision if authorised.

rows.left: Quash and remit for lawful re-exercise.
rows.right: Replace the decision with the appellate outcome.

distinctions.title: Illegality vs irrationality vs procedural impropriety
distinctions.left: Each ground targets a different legal defect.
distinctions.right: They may overlap on the same facts but should be pleaded distinctly.

rows.left: Wrong law, wrong purpose, irrelevant considerations, excess of jurisdiction.
rows.right: Focus on legal limits of power.

rows.left: Outcome no reasonable authority could reach.
Breach of natural justice or mandatory procedure.
rows.right: Fairness of process, independent of merits result.

misconceptions.trap: Judicial review is a second appeal on the merits.
misconceptions.correction: Review is supervisory. Courts test legality, not ordinary administrative preference.

misconceptions.trap: Any strict or harsh decision is Wednesbury unreasonable.
misconceptions.correction: The threshold is high: so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it.

misconceptions.trap: BSA provisions define the grounds of judicial review.
misconceptions.correction: Grounds of review arise from constitutional and administrative law; evidence law is relevant only to evidentiary questions.

cases.name: Tata Cellular v Union of India
cases.facts: The case concerned judicial review of administrative decision-making in a governmental contractual and commercial context.
cases.issue: What is the scope of judicial review over administrative discretion, particularly in commercial contexts?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court articulated limits on judicial review, emphasising examination of the decision-making process for legality and rationality rather than substitution of commercial judgment.
cases.holding: The Court applied those review standards to the administrative decision under challenge.
cases.relevance: Leading Indian authority on the scope and limits of judicial review of administrative action.

cases.name: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service
cases.facts: Civil service unions challenged a governmental decision affecting trade-union rights at GCHQ, raising the scope of reviewable administrative action.
cases.issue: What are the modern grounds of judicial review of administrative action?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The decision is associated with the modern classification of grounds of review as illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety (subject to justiciability limits).
cases.holding: The House of Lords examined the justiciability and reviewability of the decision on the facts before it.
cases.relevance: Influential comparative authority for the three classic grounds named in the topic title; Indian courts have drawn on the taxonomy while applying domestic constitutional standards. Not binding Indian precedent.

cases.name: State of Uttar Pradesh v Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh
cases.facts: The case concerned the exercise of governmental power and the standards applicable to administrative action.
cases.issue: How should courts approach challenges to the exercise of administrative or governmental power?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the legal limits on the exercise of the power and the appropriate intensity of judicial review on the facts before it.
cases.holding: The Court disposed of the appeal by applying the governing legal standards to the administrative action under challenge.
cases.relevance: Authority already present in the topic file on review of administrative power; verification remains a separate gate.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a judicial-review challenge be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the power, decision and adverse consequence. II. Test illegality (jurisdiction, purpose, considerations). III. Test irrationality / Wednesbury (high threshold). IV. Test procedural impropriety (natural justice / mandatory procedure). V. Address maintainability (standing, alternative remedy, delay). VI. Identify the precise remedy (quash, remit, declare).

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions on judicial review contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Set out the enabling power and material facts; plead distinct grounds (illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety); resist pure merits reargument; address alternative remedy and delay; and seek only the relief supported by the governing law and record.
